note: Originals used by the politics and city-life track (pol.1–7, gate-pol). Built by scripts/build_course_texts.py into course_data/texts/<id>.json. The Old Oligarch (pseudo-Xenophon, tlg0032.tlg015) is not in canonical-greekLit, so Aristotle, Ath. Pol. 27.3 (Pericles' jury pay) takes its place.

passages.title: Cleisthenes' ten tribes
passages.author: Aristotle
passages.blurb: 508/7 BC: Cleisthenes divides the citizens into ten tribes instead of four, makes a Council of five hundred, and has men named by their demes.

passages.title: The law of ostracism
passages.author: Aristotle
passages.blurb: Cleisthenes' new laws include ostracism; after Marathon the Athenians use it for the first time, against a kinsman of the tyrants.

passages.title: Pay for the jurors
passages.author: Aristotle
passages.blurb: Pericles is the first to pay the jurors, to match the private generosity of the rich Cimon.

passages.title: Jurors by lot
passages.author: Aristotle
passages.blurb: Each juror's boxwood ticket, the allotment machine, and the coloured staff that sends him to the court the lot has chosen.

passages.title: The disabled man's pension
passages.author: Lysias
passages.blurb: Before the Council a disabled craftsman answers the charge that he does not deserve his obol a day from the city.

passages.title: The Thirty and the metics
passages.author: Lysias
passages.blurb: 404 BC: the Thirty decide to arrest ten rich metics for their money; Lysias himself is seized at home while entertaining guests.

passages.title: Is Philip dead?
passages.author: Demosthenes
passages.blurb: 351 BC: Demosthenes mocks the Athenians who walk about the Agora asking for news instead of acting against Philip of Macedon.

passages.title: Peison's oath
passages.author: Lysias
passages.blurb: Lysias offers the Thirty's man a talent to save his life; Peison swears, and then takes everything in the chest.
